p: **Power** is the rate of energy transfer: P = W/t, in watt (1 W = 1 J·s⁻¹).
For a device: **P = VI**. Put R = V/I into it to get **P = I²R** and **P = V²/R**.
Choose the form that uses only what you know about **that component**.

screens.q: A question asks for “the rate of energy dissipation” in a resistor. What is it asking for?
choices: A power, in W: P = I²R.
A rate of energy dissipation is a power.
An energy, in J: W = I²Rt.
That is the trap in the Examiners’ Report 2021. A *rate* is per second: a power, in W.
Energy per second is a power, not a current.
screens.why: A rate of energy dissipation is a power: P = I²R, in W. “Energy and power were frequently confused.” (IEB Examiners’ Report 2022)

p: **Same current (series): P = I²R.** The larger resistance is brighter.
**Same pd (parallel, or a fixed supply): P = V²/R.** The smaller resistance is brighter.
The exam treats each bulb as a fixed resistance. Its brightness is its power.

rules: Same I, so P = I²R: the **larger R is brighter** (16 W against 8 W).
Same V, so P = V²/R: the **smaller R is brighter** (72 W against 36 W).
A **rating** is the power at the rated pd.

screens.q: A 2 Ω and a 4 Ω bulb are in **series** on a 12 V battery. Which is brighter?
choices: In series the current is the same, so use P = I²R: the larger R has the larger power.
Same I, so P = I²R: the larger R is brighter (16 W against 8 W).
Same current, but different resistances, so P = I²R is different.
screens.why: Same current, so P = I²R with R larger for the 4 Ω: 16 W against 8 W.

screens.q: Now the same two bulbs are in **parallel** on the 12 V battery. Which is brighter?
choices: Same V, so P = V²/R: the smaller R is brighter (72 W against 36 W).
In parallel the pd is the same, so use P = V²/R: the smaller R has the larger power.
Same pd, but different resistances, so P = V²/R is different.
screens.why: Same pd, so P = V²/R: 12²/2 = 72 W against 12²/4 = 36 W.

p: **Energy = power × time in seconds:** W = Pt, W = VIt, W = I²Rt, W = V²t/R. Energy is in joules.
A **rating** such as 220 V; 1 500 W means 1 500 J of electrical energy is transferred each second when the device is connected to 220 V.
“Heat in a time” asks for an **energy**, in J.

screens.h: Worked example 10.6: a bulb with the wrong rating
screens.q: “An electrician needs to replace a bulb that has a 220 V supply. Unfortunately, the only working light bulb in stock is rated 50 V, 100 W.” (a) “Calculate the resistance of the 50 V, 100 W light bulb.” (3) (b) “Calculate the current that should flow through the working light bulb.” (3) “The electrician uses the 50 V, 100 W light bulb and connects a resistor in series with the light bulb to ensure that the bulb operates at its correct rating when connected to the 220 V supply.” (c) “What should the resistance of the resistor be that the electrician connects in series with the light bulb?” (3)

lines.side: at the rating: 50 V and 100 W

traps: Use the bulb’s own rating, 50 V, not the 220 V supply.

lines.side: P = I²R or I = V/R also

traps: Use the bulb’s rated pd, 50 V, not 220 V.
That is the total resistance, R + 25. Take away the bulb’s 25 Ω.
R_{T} = 220 ÷ 2 = 110 Ω, and the bulb already gives 25 Ω.

lines.x: The resistor takes 220 − 50 = 170 V at 2 A, so R = 170/2 = 85,00 Ω.

why: “Operates at its correct rating”: what does that tell you?
The bulb must have 50 V across it and 100 W, so the current must be 2 A ✓. The resistor then wastes (170)(2) = 340 W, more than the bulb’s 100 W ✓.

screens.h: Worked example 10.7: power and energy in one circuit
screens.q: The 12 Ω resistor is in series in the main wire and carries the 2 A read on A₁. The 3 Ω bulb has a pd of 4,2 V across it and a current of 1,4 A through it. (a) “Calculate the power of the 12 Ω resistor.” (3) (b) “Calculate the amount of energy emitted by the 3 Ω bulb in 3 minutes.” (4)
screens.src: Adapted from IEB May 2023 P1 Q7.6 and 7.8

ask.prompt: Work out the power of the 12 Ω.

traps: The 12 Ω is in the main wire, so it carries the A₁ current, 2 A. 1,4 A is a branch current.

ask.prompt: Work out the energy in 3 minutes.

traps: Time must be in seconds. 3 minutes = 180 s.
That is the bulb’s power. “In 3 minutes” asks for an energy: multiply by 180 s.
